---
title: "Try it: two fingerprints"
---

```{python}
#| include: false
# Setup, hidden from readers. Every .qmd page starts with this same cell
# (tests/test_docs_pages.py checks). It works in a fresh folder, reads the
# example project from this repository's tests/data (offline), and defines
# sh(), which runs a command shown on the page and prints its output.
import os
import shlex
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import warnings
from pathlib import Path

import useful_views

_mirror = Path(useful_views.__file__).resolve().parents[2] / "tests" / "data"
if not (_mirror / "examples" / "pwt").is_dir():
    raise RuntimeError(f"no example data at {_mirror}")
os.environ["USEFUL_VIEWS_DATA_URL"] = str(_mirror)
os.environ.update(NO_COLOR="1", PYTHON_COLORS="0", COLUMNS="100", PYTHONUNBUFFERED="1", PYTHONIOENCODING="utf-8")
WORK = str(Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="useful-views-docs-")).resolve())
os.chdir(WORK)
warnings.formatwarning = lambda message, category, *args, **kwargs: f"{category.__name__}: {message}\n"


def sh(line, expect=0):
    """Run one command shown on the page (useful-views, cd or cat) and print
    its output as a terminal would. Fails if it exits with another code."""
    word, _, rest = line.partition(" ")
    if word == "cd":
        os.chdir(shlex.split(rest)[0])
        return
    if word == "cat":
        print(Path(shlex.split(rest)[0]).read_text(encoding="utf-8"), end="")
        return
    if word != "useful-views":
        raise ValueError(f"sh() runs useful-views, cd and cat, not {line!r}")
    done = subprocess.run(
        [sys.executable, "-m", "useful_views", *shlex.split(rest)],
        stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT, text=True, encoding="utf-8",
    )
    out = done.stdout.replace(WORK, "/path/to")
    if out.strip():
        print(out, end="")
    if done.returncode != expect:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{line!r} exited with {done.returncode}, not {expect}:\n{out}")
```

A view can have two fingerprints, a **file hash** and a **data hash**. This
page computes both by hand, in a few lines of Python, to show what each one
notices. At the end, you compare your result with useful-views' own data
hash.

| Fingerprint | Computed from | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| **File hash** | the file's bytes | Is this the very file that was recorded? |
| **Data hash** | the column names and types, and the values, in a fixed form | Does this view hold the same data as the recorded one, whoever made it? |

useful-views records the data hash of every view it makes. The file hash is
planned ([#32](https://github.com/jameshorine/useful-views/issues/32)).
[Stale views](../concepts/stale-views.md) explains what fingerprints are
for.

You need polars and pyarrow, which the [quickstart](../quickstart.qmd) setup
installs. Work in a new, empty folder. Run each block in order, in one
Python session or notebook.

## Two fingerprints

```{python}
import hashlib

import polars as pl
import pyarrow.parquet as pq


def file_hash(path):
    """SHA-256 of the file's bytes."""
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        return hashlib.sha256(f.read()).hexdigest()


def data_hash(path):
    """SHA-256 of the table's contents: the column names and types, then
    every value, whatever library wrote the file."""
    table = pq.read_table(path)
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    for field in table.schema:
        # Libraries store text as string, large_string or string_view: the same data.
        kind = "string" if "string" in str(field.type) else str(field.type)
        h.update(f"{field.name}:{kind};".encode())
    for column in table.columns:
        for value in column.to_pylist():
            h.update(repr(value).encode() + b";")
    return h.hexdigest()
```

This `data_hash` reads the whole table, value by value. That is fine for a
small example. A real one works a column at a time, and is much faster.

## The readings

Temperatures from two field sensors. One reading, station B at 06:00, was
recorded in degrees Fahrenheit by mistake. 56.8 °F is 13.8 °C.

```{python}
readings = pl.DataFrame({
    "station": ["A", "A", "B", "B"],
    "time": ["06:00", "07:00", "06:00", "07:00"],
    "temp_c": [14.2, 15.1, 56.8, None],
})
readings.write_parquet("readings.parquet")
```

## 1. The same data, saved by two libraries

Save the same table again, this time with pyarrow, as a step written with
another library would.

```{python}
pq.write_table(readings.to_arrow(), "readings_pyarrow.parquet")
print("file hash equal:", file_hash("readings.parquet") == file_hash("readings_pyarrow.parquet"))
print("data hash equal:", data_hash("readings.parquet") == data_hash("readings_pyarrow.parquet"))
```

```{python}
#| include: false
# What the text says; the build fails if it stops being true.
assert file_hash("readings.parquet") != file_hash("readings_pyarrow.parquet")
assert data_hash("readings.parquet") == data_hash("readings_pyarrow.parquet")
```


The data is the same, and the bytes differ. Each library writes its own name
into the file, and encodes and compresses the columns its own way. A library
upgrade can do the same. So the file hash alone is not enough. A file hash
recorded on your computer can differ from a co-author's for the very same
results, while the data hash matches.

## 2. The same library, saved twice

```{python}
readings.write_parquet("readings_again.parquet")
print("file hash equal:", file_hash("readings.parquet") == file_hash("readings_again.parquet"))
print("data hash equal:", data_hash("readings.parquet") == data_hash("readings_again.parquet"))
```

```{python}
#| include: false
# What the text says; the build fails if it stops being true.
assert file_hash("readings.parquet") == file_hash("readings_again.parquet")
assert data_hash("readings.parquet") == data_hash("readings_again.parquet")
```


On one computer, with the same library, the file hash is reliable. It is also
much cheaper, since it needs no understanding of the file. That makes it the
right check for "is this still the file that was recorded?"

## 3. A real change: fixing the unit error

```{python}
fixed = readings.with_columns(
    pl.when((pl.col("station") == "B") & (pl.col("time") == "06:00"))
    .then(((pl.col("temp_c") - 32) * 5 / 9).round(1))
    .otherwise(pl.col("temp_c"))
    .alias("temp_c")
)
fixed.write_parquet("readings_fixed.parquet")
print("file hash equal:", file_hash("readings.parquet") == file_hash("readings_fixed.parquet"))
print("data hash equal:", data_hash("readings.parquet") == data_hash("readings_fixed.parquet"))
```

```{python}
#| include: false
# What the text says; the build fails if it stops being true.
assert file_hash("readings.parquet") != file_hash("readings_fixed.parquet")
assert data_hash("readings.parquet") != data_hash("readings_fixed.parquet")
```


One value changed, and both fingerprints changed. Either one would tell
useful-views that a view made from the old readings is now stale.

## 4. The same rows, in another order

```{python}
fixed.reverse().write_parquet("readings_reversed.parquet")
print("data hash equal:", data_hash("readings_fixed.parquet") == data_hash("readings_reversed.parquet"))
```

```{python}
#| include: false
# What the text says; the build fails if it stops being true.
assert data_hash("readings_fixed.parquet") != data_hash("readings_reversed.parquet")
```


The same rows in another order give another data hash. Many operations
return rows in an order that can change from one run to the next, such as
`group_by` in polars (unless you pass `maintain_order=True`) and some joins.
A step that sorts its result before writing it, for example with
`.sort("station", "time")`, gives the same fingerprint every time.

## 5. The last digit of a number

Add the same three numbers in two orders, as a computation split across
several threads might:

```{python}
first = (0.1 + 0.2) + 0.3
second = 0.1 + (0.2 + 0.3)
print(first, second)
pl.DataFrame({"total": [first]}).write_parquet("total_a.parquet")
pl.DataFrame({"total": [second]}).write_parquet("total_b.parquet")
print("data hash equal:", data_hash("total_a.parquet") == data_hash("total_b.parquet"))
```

```{python}
#| include: false
# What the text says; the build fails if it stops being true.
assert (str(first), str(second)) == ("0.6000000000000001", "0.6")
assert data_hash("total_a.parquet") != data_hash("total_b.parquet")
```


Shown to a few decimal places, both are 0.6. Fingerprints are exact, so they
count the difference in the 16th digit. The two results really do differ.
Whether two numbers are close enough is a comparison with a tolerance. That
is a separate question from whether anything changed.

## 6. useful-views' own data hash

The `data_hash` above is a sketch. useful-views has the real one,
`uvs.data_hash()`. It follows exact, versioned
[rules](../reference/data-hash.md), and reads a large file a column at a
time:

```{python}
import useful_views as uvs

print(uvs.data_hash("readings.parquet"))
print(uvs.data_hash("readings.parquet") == uvs.data_hash("readings_pyarrow.parquet"))
```

```{python}
#| include: false
# What the text says; the build fails if it stops being true. The same hash
# is pinned in tests/test_data_hash.py.
assert uvs.data_hash("readings.parquet") == (
    "datahash1:sha256:76c92a8bef6fae8ffaffcd6a3558af6146eee1f608168632539e42accdebbc18"
)
assert uvs.data_hash("readings.parquet") == uvs.data_hash("readings_pyarrow.parquet")
```

Your first line should match this one character for character. The data
hash depends only on the readings, so it is the same on every computer,
whichever library wrote the file.

## What each fingerprint notices

| What happened | File hash | Data hash |
|---|---|---|
| saved by another library, or a newer version of one | usually changes | **same** |
| saved again by the same library | same | same |
| a value corrected | changes | changes |
| the same rows in another order | changes | changes |
| a number differs in its last digit | changes | changes |

The file hash is the cheap, exact check on one computer. The data hash is
the one a co-author, a reviewer or a CI job can compare, across computers
and library versions. useful-views' [stale-view
checks](../concepts/stale-views.md) are built on the data hash.
